'''Steven Allan Kivelson'''  (born May 13, 1954) is an American [[Theoretical physics|theoretical physicist]] known for several major contributions to [[condensed matter physics]]. He is the Prabhu Goel Family Professor at [[Stanford University]].<ref name=":0">{{cite web |title=Steven Kivelson Biography |url=https://history.aip.org/phn/11603025.html |accessdate=21 April 2020 |website=history.aip.org |publisher=AIP}}</ref> Before joining Stanford in 2004, he was a professor of physics at the [[University of California, Los Angeles|University of California at Los Angeles]].<ref name=":0" /> Kivelson is known for his theoretical work on [[high-temperature superconductivity]] and correlated systems.<ref name=":1" />
== Biography ==
Steven Kivelson was born in [[Boston]], [[Massachusetts]] in 1954.<ref name=":0" /> He is the son of [[Margaret Kivelson]], an emeritus professor of earth and space sciences at UCLA, and {{ill|Daniel Kivelson|de}} (1929–2003), who was a professor of chemistry, also at UCLA.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Daniel Kivelson Obituary |url=https://www.chem.ucla.edu/news/Kivelson_Obit.html |access-date=2025-05-28 |website=www.chem.ucla.edu}}</ref>

Kivelson received his Ph.D. from [[Harvard University]] in 1979, working with C. Daniel Gelatt, Jr.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |url=http://www.genealogy.ams.org/id.php?id=215250 |title=Steven Kivelson |publisher=Mathematics Genealogy Project |accessdate=March 14, 2019}}</ref><ref name=":0" /> He spent three years as a postdoctoral researcher at the [[Kavli Institute for Theoretical Physics|Institute for Theoretical Physics]] at the [[University of California, Santa Barbara]], working with [[John Robert Schrieffer]].<ref name=":1">{{cite web |last1=Biswas |first1=Sounak |last2=Kocherlakota |first2=Prashant |title=Interview: A Walk With Steven Kivelson Through the Realm of Strange Materials |url=https://science.thewire.in/the-sciences/interview-a-walk-with-steven-kivelson-through-the-realm-of-strange-materials/ |website=The Wire Science |accessdate=21 April 2020 |date=3 February 2019}}</ref><ref name=":0" />

He then joined the faculty of the [[State University of New York at Stony Brook]], where he was an assistant (1982–86), associate (1986–88) and full professor (1988–89).<ref name=":0" /> In 1988, he moved to the [[University of California, Los Angeles]].<ref name=":0" /> In 2004, Kivelson joined the faculty at [[Stanford University]], where he was appointed Prabhu Goel Family Professor of Physics in 2012.<ref name=":0" />

=== Doctoral students ===
Kivelson has advised many doctoral theses, including those of [[Assa Auerbach]] (1985),<ref name=":3" /> [[Shivaji Sondhi]] (1992)<ref name=":3" /> and [[Erica Carlson]]<ref name=":0" /> (2000).

== Research ==
In the 1995, [[Victor Emery]] and Kivelson developed the first model for [[high-temperature superconductivity]] based on the presence and fluctuations of charge stripes.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Service |first=Robert F. |date=1999-02-19 |title=Could Charge Stripes Be a Key to Superconductivity? |url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.283.5405.1106 |journal=Science |volume=283 |issue=5405 |pages=1106–1108 |doi=10.1126/science.283.5405.1106|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite book |last=Mourachkine |first=Andrei |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=9SWC9dUOj9kC&dq=kivelson+superconductivity+model&pg=PA8 |title=Room-temperature Superconductivity |date=2004 |publisher=Cambridge Int Science Publishing |isbn=978-1-904602-27-9 |language=en}}</ref> Unfortunately this model does not apply to [[Cuprate superconductor|cuprate superconductors]] due to the lack of charge–spin separation.<ref name=":2" />

In 2001, Kivelson, [[Eduardo Fradkin]], and Vadim Oganesyan developed the theory of nematic Fermi fluids.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Cabra |first1=Daniel C. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ZPZu79HU-SAC&dq=electronic+liquid+crystals+kivelson&pg=PA108 |title=Modern Theories of Many-Particle Systems in Condensed Matter Physics |last2=Honecker |first2=Andreas |last3=Pujol |first3=Pierre |date=2012-01-05 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-3-642-10449-7 |language=en}}</ref>

== Awards and honors ==
Kivelson was awarded a [[List of Guggenheim Fellowships awarded in 1995|Guggenheim Fellowship in 1995]]<ref>{{Cite web |title=Search Results - John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation |url=http://www.gf.org/fellows/results?competition=ALL&fellowship_category=ALL&lower_bound=1995&page=2&query=&upper_bound=1995&x=16&y=11 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140228013337/http://www.gf.org/fellows/results?competition=ALL&fellowship_category=ALL&lower_bound=1995&page=2&query=&upper_bound=1995&x=16&y=11 |archive-date=2014-02-28 |access-date=2025-05-28 |website=www.gf.org |language=en}}</ref> and was elected to the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] in 2001<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-04-28 |title=Steven Allan Kivelson {{!}} American Academy of Arts and Sciences |url=https://www.amacad.org/person/steven-allan-kivelson |access-date=2025-05-28 |website=www.amacad.org |language=en}}</ref> and to the [[National Academy of Sciences]] in 2010.<ref name=":0" /> In 2012, he was awarded the Bardeen prize (with Chandra Varma and [[James Sauls]]) instituted by the [[University of Illinois at Urbana–Champaign]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Communications |first=Grainger Engineering Office of Marketing and |title=Bardeen Prize |url=https://physics.illinois.edu/people/honors-and-awards/bardeen-prize |access-date=2025-05-28 |website=physics.illinois.edu |language=en}}</ref>

He earned the 2025 [[Oliver E. Buckley Prize]] of the [[American Physical Society]] for "broad and insightful theoretical contributions that have significantly advanced the understanding of correlated quantum systems".<ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-10-21 |title=Steven Kivelson receives 2025 American Physical Society prize {{!}} Stanford School of Humanities and Sciences |url=https://humsci.stanford.edu/news-post/steven-kivelson-receives-2025-american-physical-society-prize |access-date=2025-05-28 |website=humsci.stanford.edu |language=en}}</ref>
